                         EAST KENTUCKY POWER COOPERATIVE, INC.

           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 East

Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc. (“EKPC”) moves for leave to file this limited answer and

answers the September 10, 2026 answer submitted by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) in the

above-captioned proceeding. 2 EKPC’s Protest opposed PJM’s proposed revisions to its Open

Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load

Serving Entities in the PJM Region (“RAA”) to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement

(“RBP”) because the RBP Proposal is unjust and unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, inconsistent

with the Commission’s cost-causation principles and the boundaries of federal and state

jurisdiction, and contrary to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. 3 PJM’s Answer does not resolve

those defects. For the reasons set forth herein and in the EKPC Protest, EKPC respectfully requests

that the Commission reject the RBP Proposal.

implementation materials in their proper context. PJM’s Answer relies on clarifications,

           II.      BACKGROUND AND SUMMARY

           On July 31, 2026, PJM filed proposed revisions to its Tariff and RAA to establish a RBP

intended to address identified capacity shortfalls associated with forecast large-load growth.

EKPC’s Protest explained that a legitimate reliability objective does not excuse a rate design that

fails to make costs, credits, collateral obligations, and default risks transparent, traceable,

administrable, and reasonably tied to the entities that caused or benefit from the procurement. 10

PJM’s proposed fallback allocation still spreads RBP costs to load without demonstrating that the

charged LSEs caused the procurement need or receive commensurate benefits. Its disparate

treatment of FRR entities and RPM self-supply LSEs remains unexplained. And severing one

credit-rate input leaves unresolved the nature, timing, quantity, release, and default treatment of

the exposure being collateralized.

           III.      LIMITED ANSWER

                     A. PJM Has Not Carried Its Affirmative Burden Under FPA Section 205.

           Section 205 places the burden squarely on PJM to show that the RBP is just and reasonable.

All jurisdictional rates and all rules and practices affecting them must be just and reasonable and

not unduly discriminatory or preferential, and when a public utility proposes a change, “the burden

of proof to show that the increased rate or charge is just and reasonable shall be upon the public

utility.” 14 The Commission’s regulations accordingly require a filing utility to submit the

information necessary to explain and support the proposed change. 15 The distinction from section

206 of the FPA is fundamental: PJM is not defending an existing rate presumed lawful against an

EKPC complaint; PJM is asking the Commission to authorize new tariff provisions. 16 PJM itself

has publicly described the governing rule the same way: a public utility making a section 205 filing

“has the legal burden of demonstrating” that its proposed change is just and reasonable. 17

           To satisfy this burden requires more than showing that a reliability problem exists or that

PJM’s preferred mechanism is administratively convenient. PJM must connect the evidence to the

specific rate design for which it seeks approval. And the Commission must evaluate the proposal

actually filed on the record before it, provide a reasoned explanation for its conclusion, and respond

                    B. PJM Failed to Address EKPC’s Cost Causation Arguments.

           Cost causation is not a subsidiary policy preference that the Commission may bypass once

PJM does not carry that principle through the RBP Proposal.

                   C. EKPC’s Protest Is Consistent with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.

an RBP process to ensure LSEs responsible to provide retail service to Large Loads subscribed to

the procurement process so the appropriate amount of capacity is procured. As noted above, this

would have provided greater certainty, better aligned cost causation, and provided ratepayer

protection by ensuring the appropriate LSEs are charged the costs they were directly responsible

for incurring. EKPC protested the RBP because, as proposed, the RBP may shift those costs to

                    D. PJM Does Not Justify Disparate Treatment of FRR Entities and RPM Self

entities may have taken materially similar planning actions to satisfy aggregate resource

insulating one portfolio while disregarding the other.

V.   THE QUANTITY ON WHICH COLLATERAL IS REQUIRED IS NOT DEFINED
37. An LSE cannot calculate its posting unless the tariff identifies the controlling megawatt
    quantity. Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.8(b)(i)(A) requires collateral equal
    to the RBP Credit Rate multiplied by “RBP UCAP MW committed.” The amount of the
    requirement therefore depends entirely on that quantity. PJM’s Answer and its
    implementation materials leave three questions about it unresolved: whether the megawatts
    must be in service; whether an individual LSE’s posting follows the megawatts its Electric
    Distributor assigns or is scaled to the Final RBP Target; and what quantity applies, if any,
    where the Electric Distributor reports nothing.
        A. Whether the megawatts must be in service
38. PJM’s Answer states that “no collateral would be required for RBP Resources [that] are
    not in service for that Delivery Year.” PJM Answer at 78 n.234.
39. That in-service limitation does not appear in section 18.8(b)(i)(A). That provision defines
    the quantity as “the amount of RBP UCAP MW that receives a commitment through the
    Reliability Backstop Procurement minus each commitment of RBP UCAP MW that is
    rescinded pursuant to Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.6(e).” Commitments received,
    less rescissions. There is no in-service condition, and PJM has proposed no revision to that
    provision.
40. Rescission under section 18.6(e) occurs only “where RBP UCAP MW fail to come online
    for three Delivery Years beginning with the first Delivery Year in which the RBP Resource
    was committed.” A resource that has not achieved commercial operation therefore remains
    within the quantity for up to three Delivery Years. PJM’s transmittal describes the same
    mechanic and identifies rescission as the operative event: the input “will change as
    committed resources fail to follow through on their commitment and do not achieve
    commercial operation,” and it is the rescinded commitment that “is subtracted from the
    input used to determine the uniform RBP credit requirement.” July 31 Filing at 116.

 41. The September 14 Presentation states the Answer’s position on one slide and applies the
    tariff definition on another. Slide 9 defines the quantity as “the level of RBP UCAP MW
    for which an LSE is allocated cost responsibility submitted for the buyer by the EDC,” and
    adds in a note that “Committed MW is equal to the generation that is coming online for
    that delivery year.”
42. Example #4 at slide 57 of the September 14 Presentation does the opposite. It addresses a
    unit that “does not come online for Delivery Year.” The example carries Committed MW
    (UCAP) of 50 throughout, assesses the RBP Shortfall Charge on all 50 committed
    megawatts under section 18.6(d), and computes RBP Credits on Daily Owned MW of zero.
    The commitment remains at 50 megawatts and settlement occurs on that quantity even
    though the resource is not in service. That is the filed definition, applied.
43. The two formulas use different quantities. RBP Credits, and therefore the RBP Charges
    assessed to load, are computed on Daily Owned MW, which is why the charge is zero in
    Example #4. The collateral requirement in section 18.8(b)(i)(A) is computed on RBP
    UCAP MW committed, which in the same example remains 50. The absence of a charge
    in a Delivery Year is a result of the credit formula. It does not change the quantity to which
    the Credit Rate applies.
         B. Whether the posting follows assigned megawatts or the Final RBP Target
44. Section 18.8(b)(i)(A) sets the cumulative RBP credit requirement for all LSEs as the Credit
    Rate multiplied by committed megawatts. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(1) sets each individual
    LSE’s posting as $1.5 million multiplied by the RBP Obligation MW its Electric
    Distributor submits, “scaled, as necessary, in the event that the RBP Obligation MW values
    uploaded by the Electric Distributor do not sum to the fixed, Final RBP Target MW for the
    zone/area.”
45. Those provisions use different quantities, and PJM states the procurement may clear short
    of the Final RBP Target. Where it does, committed megawatts are fewer than the Target.
    The individual postings scaled to the Target under (B)(1) would then sum to more than the
    cumulative requirement calculated on committed megawatts under (A). Because the Credit
    Rate is $1.5 million per megawatt, each 100 megawatts of difference between the two
    quantities changes the aggregate amount posted by $150 million.
46. PJM has identified each quantity as governing. Footnote 234 states that the amount “would
    be based on the RBP UCAP MW committed for that Delivery Year.” PJM’s written
    response of August 14, 2026 stated that the Final RBP Target governs.
         C. What applies where the Electric Distributor reports nothing
47. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(2) provides that where no RBP Obligations are reported for an
    Electric Distributor zone or area, LSEs serving load there “may be required to post”
    collateral calculated on “the [LSE’s] pro-rata share of the Daily Unforced Capacity
    Obligation for the zone/area as determined in RAA, Schedule 8.” The September 14
    Presentation states that measure at slide 70, while a footnote to the example at slide 69
    describes the same fallback as a Peak Load Contribution allocation.
48. The provision is permissive, and PJM confirmed in writing on September 15, 2026 that it
    admits more than one outcome. An LSE may be required to post at the Credit Rate, may
    post at the Credit Rate and additionally be assessed under the Unreasonable Credit Risk
                                               9
      provisions of Attachment Q, Section II, or may not be required to post at the Credit Rate
     but be subject to an unreasonable credit risk assessment. The provision states that an LSE
     “may be required to post.” It does not state that a Credit Rate posting is required in every
     case in which no RBP Obligations are reported.
49. The quantity also changes basis. Under (B)(1) an LSE posts on megawatts attributed to it
    through the allocation process. Under (B)(2) it posts on its share of total load. An entity
    with no RBP Obligation under section 18.3 has no requirement under (B)(1) and a
    requirement measured by its entire load under (B)(2).
50. Subsection (B)(2) is also difficult to square with PJM’s defense of the uniform rate. PJM
    states that its methodology “is based on the committed obligation itself and avoids having
    the adequacy of the credit protection depend upon long-range predictions about individual
    LSE’s financials.” PJM Answer at 82. The Unreasonable Credit Risk provisions of
    Attachment Q, Section II are an individualized assessment of a participant’s financial
    condition. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(2) routes directly into them, and PJM has confirmed that
    an assessment may be made in place of, or in addition to, a Credit Rate posting. PJM has
    therefore built individualized credit evaluation into the construct. It applies where an
    Electric Distributor fails to report, and not where the Electric Distributor reports.
        D. Timing
51. Section 18.3(b)(iii) requires the initial allocation to be reported no later than sixty days
    before the Delivery Year, and collateral is due prior to forty-five days before. An LSE
    would have approximately fifteen days between learning which subsection applies to it,
    and on what quantity, and funding the requirement.
52. The timing differs from the forward-exposure rationale. PJM relies on the long-dated
    character of the obligation to distinguish it from Peak Market Activity, while requiring no
    security until shortly before the first applicable Delivery Year. The near-term exposure is
    determined well before then.
53. Both of the first two Delivery Years are subject to the price collar PJM extended through

54. At the $555.00/MW-day maximum willingness to pay, the differential is therefore
    $230.00/MW-day for 2028/2029 and $217.17/MW-day for 2029/2030, or $83,950 and
    $79,267 per MW respectively. The two-year total is $163,217 per MW, which on an

                                             10
      determined once the 2029/2030 auction clears in December 2026, and no collateral is
     required against it until approximately April 17, 2028.
55. Opinion. An LSE cannot determine from the filed rate the quantity on which it must post.
    The tariff, the Answer, and the implementation presentation give different answers to
    whether the megawatts must be in service, and PJM’s own settlement example applies the
    tariff definition rather than the Answer’s. PJM has identified both committed megawatts
    and the Final RBP Target as governing an individual posting. And where an Electric
    Distributor reports nothing, whether an entity posts at all, on what quantity, and whether it
    is additionally assessed for unreasonable credit risk are matters the filed provisions leave

VI. THE EXPOSURE THE REQUIREMENT SECURES IS LARGELY ORDINARY
    RPM ACTIVITY
        A. Coordination with Attachment Q
56. PJM proposes to delete the sentence providing that settlement of cleared RBP positions
    “may be included, as appropriate, in Peak Market Activity,” on the basis that it could cause
    confusion that RBP Charges may be captured in that calculation.
57. Removal of the clause does not establish how an invoiced RBP billing line item is excluded
    from the Peak Market Activity calculation in Attachment Q, section VII.A, and PJM has
    proposed no conforming revision to Attachment Q. Three provisions are unaffected by the
    deletion and bear on the coordination question. Nothing in section 18 supersedes
    Attachment Q. The RBP requirements are separate from and additional to credit
    requirements arising under Attachment Q. And under sections 18.8(b)(i)(B)(1) and (B)(2),
    PJM may evaluate an LSE for unreasonable credit risk under Attachment Q, Section II and
    require additional RBP Collateral, which as set out at paragraph 47 above may be done in
    addition to, or in place of, a Credit Rate posting.
58. PJM explains the separate requirement as securing the forward RPM component of the
    obligation together with the contract-for-differences amount, on the ground that Peak
    Market Activity does not prospectively collateralize the RPM component over the term.
    The RBP settles economically through RPM and a contract-for-differences: load pays the
    RPM clearing price through ordinary capacity billing and pays or receives the difference
    through the new billing line item.

68. Opinion. PJM’s illustration shows collateral held flat for eight of fifteen Delivery Years

VIII. RECOMMENDATIONS FOR ADDITIONAL PROCEEDINGS
69. PJM has consented to the Commission resolving the buyer-side Credit Rate through
    additional procedures, and states that the buyer-side rules need not be effective for the
    Reliability Backstop Procurement to be conducted. The matters set out below should be
    resolved on a schedule that reflects when the underlying exposure becomes measurable,
    which, as set out in paragraph 5, is well before the filed posting date.
70. In my opinion, any additional procedures should define the exposure the requirement is
    intended to secure and the quantity and timing of that exposure before a replacement Credit
    Rate is selected. That includes the relationship among the RPM component of the payment,
    the contract-for-differences amount created by the RBP, the reallocation provided by
    section 18.9(a), and any residual exposure under Operating Agreement section 15.2.2. It
    also requires a defined meaning of “RBP UCAP MW committed” and its relationship to
    megawatts in service, megawatts allocated to an LSE, RBP Obligation MW reported by an
    Electric Distributor, and the Final RBP Target. The procedures should also establish when
    the resulting exposure arises and when collateral is required in relation to it.
71. The methodology should then provide objective standards for recalculating and releasing
    collateral as the relevant conditions change, including the RBP commitment price,
    observed RPM clearing prices and resulting contract-for-differences amounts, remaining
    tenor, committed quantity, and participant credit condition. It should also establish the

                                             13
     order in which collateral, the reallocation under section 18.9(a), and any mutualization
    under Operating Agreement section 15.2.2 apply, so that the residual loss the collateral is
    intended to secure can be identified.
72. PJM’s Answer and implementation materials supply explanations that were not available
    when I submitted my original affidavit. They do not establish the relationship between the
    collateral required and the exposure secured.
73. The question presented by the buyer-side credit requirement is therefore not whether $1.5
    million per MW is too high or too low. It is whether the amount, the quantity, the timing,
    the recalculation, the release, and the default treatment of collateral bear a defined
    relationship to the exposure the requirement is intended to secure. On the present record
    they do not.
